beats.trigger: From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new, this is the title

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent.
beats.got: you share context, a skill, output or an interface, not the agent itself, and picking one is a strategy call

beats.trigger: Bring one example from your own organisation where people got access to a tool and did not use it.
beats.got: nothing new. I already know ours: the confluence bot nobody opened after week two

beats.trigger: Test the switch assumptions and name one person and one test to take out of the room
beats.got: nothing new, just the list. 'one person' sounds small for what I want to build

beats.trigger: What would you want a teammate to have: your `memory/` folder, one of your skills, the morning output, or a way to ask the agent a question in Slack?
beats.got: I would pick the slack interface first. I haven't really thought about the other three as separate options

beats.trigger: Hold the impulse.
beats.got: my reflex is 'ship it to everyone', and the module says start from the teammate's job. Jobs-to-be-done is old but I haven't applied it to agents

beats.trigger: This is a heavy read across the working set, and a shallow confident finish is as risky as over-reading.
beats.got: nothing new. I pasted the prompt, glanced at jtbd.md and it looked fine. Skipped the specificity check

beats.trigger: "Share the whole agent" is a vendor pitch and is NOT on the list.
beats.got: four shapes, and the whole agent isn't one of them. That matches why my 'just give them the setup' idea keeps stalling

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: nothing new, it's a hand-off to the next exercise

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: next step is to find what blocks people from using it, then plan the tech and the people side

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: pick the obstacle that keeps the others hard, not the first technical limit I see. I always fix the technical one first

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: my people plan was mostly UNASSIGNED, and that is the finding. I had not checked who maintains anything

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact to `module-7/monday.md`
beats.got: nothing new, just the hand-off again

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: nothing new. The plans are guesses until someone tests them

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: 'fire their current hire' is a sharp way to frame adoption. The competitor is the spreadsheet or the colleague they already use

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: the agent wrote three ways my sales rollout dies, and they were believable. This is the part I would have skipped on my own

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.
beats.got: I pick by what I can build fast. That is shopping, apparently

beats.trigger: Lecture: Access is not absorption
beats.got: nothing new, the lecture title

beats.trigger: Access is a switch somebody flips, and it completes in a minute.
beats.got: licence counts and adoption are reported as one number, and they are different things. I know this from our own rollouts but hadn't said it

beats.trigger: The leadership had not done the analysis.
beats.got: a multi-agent value-stream redesign, a good workshop, and the leadership shrugged because they hadn't done the analysis themselves. That is the org-wide failure I haven't met

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: you can copy context, boundary and checks in an afternoon, but the person who answers for the agent doesn't copy. That is my maintenance blocker

beats.trigger: Pick the one your teammate's week can take in.
beats.got: each of the four asks something different of the receiver. Mostly a recap of the exercise

beats.trigger: Your candidate is not competing with nothing.
beats.got: the answers to 'what would have to be true' come back small, like where they look and who has vouched for it. I had been aiming at big

beats.trigger: Have the conversation before you build anything more.
beats.got: talk to one person before building more. I don't love it because building is what I do, but it is probably right

beats.trigger: Who gets your context, who gets a skill, who wants only the output, and who would use an @mention?
beats.got: it is rarely the same person for all four. I pasted the prompt and moved on

beats.trigger: Access is a switch someone flips. Absorption happens in other people's weeks.
beats.got: nothing new, a recap of what I just did

beats.trigger: Their answer is the evidence. The plan is still the hypothesis.
beats.got: I need to bring back what the named person said, not just the plan

beats.trigger: What if you didn't have to build each one by hand?
beats.got: the next module is about not building every agent by hand. That is the one I'm here for

take_homes: Don't ship the setup to the sales team on spec. Ask one person how they do the job today and what they use now.
The thing that doesn't copy is who answers for it. Name the maintainer before building.
Access and absorption are different numbers, and I only ever track access.

monday.move: Ask one person in sales how they pull together their weekly pipeline today, and ask what would have to be true for them to drop what they use. Build nothing before that.
monday.who: the head of sales ops (I will pick the actual person from the people-plan gaps)
monday.when: Monday, 30 minutes, before I touch the weekend setup
monday.stop_condition: If they say what they have works and they don't want it, I stop and don't build the sales version
monday.blocker: Nobody in sales asked for this and I haven't found who would maintain it. The conversation may just confirm that.

misconception.why: The module was about sharing, not checking, and I skipped the specificity and branch checks and the outputs looked fine to me. The failure stories and the people plan full of unassigned names were useful, but that is about adoption, not about the agent's output. I'd still say checking is mostly for beginners.

one_line: Good for anyone about to roll out agents to non-engineers, because it makes you ask who will actually use it before you build. The first half is slow if you already run agents, and I skipped most of the checks.
